parts.note: newshounds, collectively, are the media

explanation.surface: An English girl trails after the press pack, who come from far away.
explanation.definitionFit: Something dating from the Middle Ages belongs to a period far in the past.

clue.text: Wine imbibed by nearly a majority of Georgian ruffians

indicators.note: imbibed by says the wine is swallowed inside the other piece
nearly means the word for a majority loses its last letter

explanation.surface: Most Georgians, drinking wine, become hooligans.
explanation.walkthrough: MOST shortened by 'nearly' gives MOS, which takes in HOCK. 'Georgian' means of the 18th-century reigns of the Georges, not the country.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mohocks were gangs of aristocratic thugs terrorising London streets around 1712.

clue.text: Some bard antedating Petrarch

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A poet who came before Petrarch.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'Petrarch' as the definition, but Dante is not Petrarch: the whole clue defines him, the poet who preceded Petrarch, while 'Some' picks him out of 'bard antedating'.
explanation.definitionFit: Dante, the Florentine poet of the Divine Comedy, died in 1321, when Petrarch was still a young man.

clue.text: Faculty endowing auditory receptiveness for starters

indicators.note: for starters says take the opening letter of each of the three words

explanation.surface: A sense that grants a listener's openness to sound, to begin with.
explanation.definitionFit: Hearing is one of the senses or faculties, as in having an ear for music.

clue.text: A governess primarily with energy blown about the start of spring

definitions.text: A governess primarily with energy blown about the start of spring

indicators.note: primarily means only the first letter of governess is used
about says the rearranged letters go round the next piece
blown suggests the letters of energy scattered by the wind into a new order
the start of says only the opening letter of spring is taken

explanation.surface: A governess, full of vigour, is swept along at the beginning of spring.
explanation.walkthrough: ENERGY rearranged ('blown') gives NEGREY, which goes 'about' S to make NESGREY, after A and G. The whole clue describes the title heroine of Anne Brontë's novel, herself a governess.
explanation.definitionFit: Anne Brontë's 1847 novel follows the life of a young woman who takes work teaching children of wealthy families.

clue.text: After start of play the whole story is revealed

indicators.note: After places the word for the whole behind the first letter of play
start of says only the opening letter of play is wanted

parts.note: the lot means everything, the whole

explanation.surface: Once the play starts, the full narrative comes out.
explanation.definitionFit: A plot is the storyline or sequence of events in a narrative.

clue.text: E.g. Don Giovanni, a macho chap that's leading a piece about Seville initially

i.e. is the abbreviation for 'that is'

indicators.note: initially says only the first letter of Seville is used

parts.note: a man is a piece in chess or draughts

explanation.surface: Don Giovanni is a swaggering fellow at the head of a play about Seville.
explanation.walkthrough: Don Giovanni is set in Seville, so 'about Seville' looks like a description of the opera; only its first letter matters. 'about' is a link here.
explanation.definitionFit: Don Giovanni, Mozart's seducer, is the archetype of a womaniser who charms the opposite sex.

clue.text: Isolde's head lost in coach embracing leading man

indicators.note: embracing says the shortened coach word wraps round the next piece
lost in says a letter goes missing from the word for coach

parts.note: a coach on the railway is part of a train

parts.note: leading means first, written 1st, with the 1 read as I

explanation.surface: Isolde loses her head in a carriage while hugging the hero of the opera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leading man' looks like the definition, but 'leading' gives 1st (read as IST) and 'man' alone defines; 'lost in' drops Isolde's first letter from the coach word.
explanation.definitionFit: Tristan is the male hero of the Arthurian legend and of Wagner's opera, Isolde's lover.

clue.text: One who governed Sparta finally

parts.note: one who governed led, a past tense of lead

indicators.note: finally says only the closing letter of Sparta is taken

explanation.surface: A ruler of Sparta, at last.
explanation.walkthrough: Leda was queen of Sparta as wife of King Tyndareus; 'One' merely introduces her.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Leda was the Spartan queen seduced by Zeus in the form of a swan.

clue.text: Girl's memory was famously jogged by one of these?

definitions.text: memory was famously jogged by one of these
definitions.meaning: in Proust a small shell-shaped cake dipped in tea brings the narrator's childhood flooding back

explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe is ignored, as usual in crosswords: the girl's name with its possessive s gives the same letters as the plural of the cakes.
explanation.definitionFit: Madeleine is a girl's name, and the little sponge cakes of that name are the trigger of involuntary memory in Proust's novel.

clue.text: Therefore Hindu god displaces European in bar

indicators.note: displaces says one piece pushes out another and takes its place

parts.note: hence means therefore

explanation.surface: So a Hindu deity ousts a European from a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: INDRA replaces the first E of HENCE to give H-INDRA-NCE. 'bar' looks like a pub but means an obstacle.
explanation.definitionFit: A bar in the sense of a barrier or impediment is an obstruction.

clue.text: Old Irish king seen in Granard, right?

indicators.note: seen in says the answer lies inside the words that follow, spanning the comma

explanation.surface: Was an ancient Irish ruler spotted in the Longford town of Granard?
explanation.walkthrough: Granard is a town in County Longford, Ireland, so the surface keeps an Irish setting.
explanation.definitionFit: Ard ri is Irish for high king, the title of the overlord of early medieval Ireland.

clue.text: Acres mostly confused by Malaprop initially implying a word meaning "paragon"

indicators.note: confused says the shortened word's letters are mixed up
mostly means Acres loses its final letter
initially says only the first letter of Malaprop is used

explanation.surface: Bob Acres, flustered by Mrs Malaprop, hints at a word for a model of excellence.
explanation.walkthrough: Acres and Mrs Malaprop are both characters in Sheridan's comedy The Rivals, which explains the surface. ACRE ('mostly') rearranged ('confused') gives CREA.
explanation.definitionFit: The cream of something is its finest part, so a person who is the cream is a model of excellence.

clue.text: One taken in by fairy mostly going wild about Welsh stories

indicators.note: taken in by says the numeral one is held inside the rest

parts.note: Queen Mab is the fairy of English folklore described in Romeo and Juliet

indicators.note: wild says the shortened letters are thrown into disorder
mostly means going loses its final letter

parts.note: taken as written before trimming
on means about, concerning
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone is taken in by a fairy running riot over Welsh tales.
explanation.walkthrough: Queen Mab is the fairy midwife of Mercutio's speech in Romeo and Juliet. 'taken in by' places the one just after the fairy, inside the whole.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mabinogion is the collection of medieval prose tales from Wales.

clue.text: Male at end of scene exited right of the audience

parts.note: left means exited, departed

explanation.surface: A man walks off at the close of a scene, moving to the audience's right.
explanation.walkthrough: Stage directions are given from the actor's viewpoint facing the audience, so the actor's left is the audience's right.
explanation.definitionFit: The side of a stage to the actor's left, facing the house, is the spectators' right-hand side.

clue.text: "With a mighty effort I drove my right elbow and shoulder against the —" (John Buchan, Mr Standfast)

explanation.definitionFit: A sidebar is a side panel or rail, the word Buchan used in that scene of his wartime spy thriller.

explanation.definitionFit: Boccaccio's Decameron is a 14th-century collection of a hundred tales, some notably ribald.

clue.text: A cowherd to start with, turning back on hellish demon?

definitions.text: A cowherd to start with, turning back on hellish demon?

hellish suggests the letters of demon are put into turmoil

explanation.surface: A herdsman who, early on, turned away from a fiend.
explanation.walkthrough: A and C turned back give CA; 'hellish' rearranges DEMON to EDMON. Bede says Caedmon was an illiterate cowherd granted the gift of religious song in a dream.
explanation.definitionFit: Caedmon, the earliest named English poet, was a cowherd at Whitby Abbey who turned to sacred verse.

clue.text: One of Wyndham's mutants, Miss Guthrie we hear laid out

explanation.definitionFit: In John Wyndham's novel The Chrysalids, the telepathic children hiding their difference are known by this term.

clue.text: Londoner about to meet a Yorkshire artist with no husband

explanation.definitionFit: A Cockney is a working-class native of London's East End.

clue.text: Pilgrim in church with a bogus cure

explanation.definitionFit: Chaucer casts himself as one of the travellers to Canterbury in his Tales.

clue.text: "I have — a Preface, while I professed to write a Dedication" (Dedication to Tom Jones)
